name: Weighted mean (two values)
description: Computes the weighted average of two values x1 and x2 with weights w1 and w2, using (w1·x1 + w2·x2)/(w1 + w2). Values with larger weights pull the average toward themselves.
notes: The weights need not sum to 1 because the formula divides by their total. If both weights are equal this reduces to the ordinary arithmetic mean.

name: Arithmetic mean (two values)
description: Computes the arithmetic mean of two values a and b as their sum divided by two, (a + b)/2. It is the ordinary average and lies exactly halfway between the two values.
notes: The result always falls between the two inputs. For quantities like rates or ratios, the geometric or harmonic mean may be more appropriate.

name: Harmonic mean (two values)
description: Computes the harmonic mean of two values a and b as 2ab/(a + b). It is the appropriate average for rates such as speeds over equal distances.
notes: Both values should be positive and nonzero. The harmonic mean is always the smallest of the three classic means, at or below the geometric and arithmetic means.

name: Weighted mean (3 values)
description: Computes the weighted mean of three values x1, x2, x3 with weights w1, w2, w3 as (w1*x1 + w2*x2 + w3*x3)/(w1 + w2 + w3). Larger weights pull the average toward their associated values.
notes: The sum of the weights must not be zero. Weights need not add up to 1; the denominator normalizes them automatically.

name: Harmonic mean (3 values)
description: Computes the harmonic mean of three values a, b, c as 3 divided by the sum of their reciprocals, 3/(1/a + 1/b + 1/c). It is the appropriate average for rates such as speeds over equal distances.
notes: None of a, b, c may be zero, and typically all are positive. The harmonic mean is always less than or equal to the arithmetic mean.

name: Geometric mean (3 values)
description: Computes the geometric mean of three values a, b, c as the cube root of their product, cbrt(a*b*c). It is the central tendency suited to quantities that combine multiplicatively, such as growth rates.
notes: Values should be positive for the mean to be meaningful. The geometric mean never exceeds the arithmetic mean of the same values.

name: Average of 3
description: Computes the arithmetic mean of three values as (a+b+c)÷3. The result is the single value that, repeated three times, gives the same total.
notes: This is a simple unweighted mean of exactly three numbers; each value counts equally. For different weights, use a weighted average instead.

name: Percentage change
description: Computes the percentage change from an old value to a new value using (new−old)÷old×100. A positive result is an increase, a negative result a decrease.
notes: Change is relative to the old value, which must be nonzero. The sign shows direction; this differs from percentage-point change.

name: Weighted average (2)
description: Computes the weighted mean of two values as (v1×w1+v2×w2)÷(w1+w2), giving an average where each value contributes in proportion to its weight.
notes: Weights need not sum to any particular total; only their ratio matters. The sum of weights must be nonzero. Equal weights reduce to a plain average.

name: Range (max − min)
expression: max(a, b, c) - min(a, b, c)
description: Computes the statistical range of three values as the largest minus the smallest, max(a,b,c)−min(a,b,c). It measures how spread out the values are.
notes: The range uses only the extreme values, so it is sensitive to outliers and ignores the middle value. The result is never negative.

name: Coefficient of variation
description: Divides the standard deviation by the mean and multiplies by 100 to give the coefficient of variation as a percentage, expressing relative variability independent of the unit of measurement.
notes: Meaningful only when the mean is positive and on a ratio scale with a true zero. It lets you compare dispersion across datasets with different units or very different means.

name: Mean of 2 values
description: Adds two values and divides by two to give their arithmetic mean, the simple average lying exactly midway between the two numbers.
notes: The result always falls between the two inputs. It weights both values equally; use a weighted average if they represent different sample sizes or importance.

name: Mean of 4 values
description: Sums four values and divides by four to give their arithmetic mean, the average value of the four numbers.
notes: All four values are weighted equally. The mean is sensitive to outliers, so a single extreme value can shift it noticeably.

name: Mean of 5 values
description: Sums five values and divides by five to give their arithmetic mean, the average of the five numbers.
notes: All five values are weighted equally. The mean is affected by outliers; consider the median if the data are skewed.

name: Weighted average of 3
description: Multiplies each of three values by its weight, sums the products, and divides by the total weight to give the weighted average, an average that counts each value in proportion to its weight.
notes: Total weight must not be zero. Weights need not sum to 1 since the division normalizes them; larger weights pull the result toward the corresponding value.

name: Population variance of 3 values
description: Computes the population variance of three values as the mean of the squared deviations from their average. It quantifies how far the three values spread from their mean.
notes: This divides by n (3), the population form; the sample variance divides by n − 1 instead. Units are the square of the input units, so take the square root for a comparable spread.

name: Population standard deviation of 3
description: Takes the square root of the population variance of three values, giving the population standard deviation, a measure of spread expressed in the same units as the data.
notes: This uses the population form dividing by n (3); the sample version divides by n − 1. Unlike variance, the result shares the units of the original values.

name: Percentile rank position
description: Estimates the rank position corresponding to a given percentile in an ordered list of n items, using p/100 times (n+1). It locates where the percentile falls among the ranked data.
notes: Percentile p is on a 0-to-100 scale. The result is often fractional, meaning the value lies between two data points and must be interpolated; several percentile conventions exist besides (n+1).

name: Geometric mean of 2
description: Takes the square root of the product of two values to give their geometric mean, the central value appropriate for quantities that combine multiplicatively, such as growth rates.
notes: Both values should be positive for a meaningful result. The geometric mean is always less than or equal to the arithmetic mean and suits ratios or rates better than sums.

name: Geometric mean of 3
description: Takes the cube root of the product of three values to give their geometric mean, the multiplicative central value of the three numbers.
notes: All three values should be positive. Like the two-value case, it is suited to averaging growth factors or ratios rather than additive quantities.

name: Harmonic mean of 2
description: Computes the harmonic mean of two values as twice their product divided by their sum. It is the appropriate average for rates, such as speeds over equal distances.
notes: Values should be positive and their sum non-zero. The harmonic mean is always the smallest of the three Pythagorean means and is dominated by the smaller value.

name: Root mean square of 2
description: Computes the root mean square of two values as the square root of the mean of their squares. The RMS gives a magnitude-based average that weights larger values more heavily.
notes: Because it squares the inputs, sign is ignored and the result is always non-negative and at least as large as the arithmetic mean of the magnitudes.

name: Pearson correlation from components
description: Computes the Pearson correlation coefficient from summary components: the sum of cross products divided by the square root of the product of the two sums of squares. It measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship.
notes: Inputs are the (mean-centered) sums of products and squares, not raw data. The result lies between −1 and +1; near 0 means little linear association, and it captures linear relationships only.

name: Combined mean of 2 groups
description: Computes the overall mean of two groups by weighting each group's mean by its size, summing, and dividing by the total count. It gives the pooled mean as if the two groups were merged.
notes: Weights are the group sizes, so the larger group influences the result more. Total size must be positive; averaging the two group means directly is wrong unless the groups are equal in size.

name: Pooled Standard Deviation
description: Computes the pooled standard deviation of two samples, sqrt(((n1-1)*s1^2 + (n2-1)*s2^2)/(n1+n2-2)), a weighted combination of the two sample standard deviations. It estimates a common spread assumed shared by both groups.
notes: It assumes the two populations have equal variances. Sample sizes n1 and n2 must each be at least 2 so the denominator n1+n2-2 stays positive.

name: Regression Slope
description: Computes the slope of the least-squares regression line by dividing the sum of cross-products Sxy by the sum of squared x-deviations Sxx. The slope indicates how much y changes per unit increase in x.
notes: Sxy and Sxx are sums of deviations from the means, not raw sums. Sxx must be positive; a slope near zero implies little linear relationship between x and y.

name: Regression Intercept
description: Computes the y-intercept of the least-squares regression line as the mean of y minus the slope times the mean of x. This ensures the fitted line passes through the point of means (x̄, ȳ).
notes: Requires the slope b to already be estimated. The intercept is the predicted y when x=0, which may lie outside the observed data range and lack real meaning.

name: Pearson Correlation r
description: Computes the Pearson correlation coefficient by dividing the covariance Sxy by the product of the standard deviations of x and y. The result measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship.
notes: The value ranges from -1 to +1; near 0 means weak linear association. Correlation does not imply causation and captures only linear, not curved, relationships.

name: Coefficient of Determination
description: Squares the correlation coefficient r to give R², the proportion of variance in the dependent variable explained by the linear model. A value of 0.72, for example, means 72% of the variation is explained.
notes: R² lies between 0 and 1 and is always non-negative even for negative r. It never decreases when predictors are added, so a high R² alone does not confirm a good model.

name: Covariance of Two Points
description: Computes the covariance of two data points by averaging the products of each point's deviations from the mean of x and mean of y. A positive result indicates x and y tend to move together.
notes: This divides by 2 (population form for two points), not n-1. With only two points the result is limited and mainly illustrative of how covariance is built.

name: Percentile Rank
description: Computes the percentile rank of a value as the count of scores below it plus half the count equal to it, divided by the total count n, expressed as a percentage. It shows the relative standing of a value in a dataset.
notes: Uses the midpoint convention for ties (half of equal scores counted). The result ranges from 0 to 100%; n must equal the total number of observations.

name: Interquartile Range (IQR)
description: Computes the interquartile range as the third quartile Q3 minus the first quartile Q1. The IQR is the spread of the middle 50% of the data and is a robust measure of dispersion.
notes: Q3 must be at least Q1, so the result is non-negative. Being based on quartiles, the IQR resists outliers, unlike the full range or standard deviation.

name: Geometric Mean (2 values)
description: Computes the geometric mean of two values as the square root of their product. It is the appropriate average for ratios, rates, or multiplicative quantities such as growth factors.
notes: Both values must be positive; a zero or negative input makes the result zero or undefined. The geometric mean is always less than or equal to the arithmetic mean.

name: Harmonic Mean (2 values)
description: Computes the harmonic mean of two values as 2 divided by the sum of their reciprocals. It is the correct average for rates such as speeds over equal distances.
notes: Both values must be nonzero and are typically positive. The harmonic mean is always the smallest of the harmonic, geometric, and arithmetic means for positive numbers.

name: Root Mean Square (3 values)
description: Computes the root mean square of three values as the square root of the average of their squares. The RMS gives the effective magnitude and is used for quantities like AC voltage or deviations.
notes: Because values are squared, signs do not affect the result, so RMS is always non-negative. It is always greater than or equal to the arithmetic mean of the magnitudes.

name: Pearson Median Skewness
description: Computes Pearson's second skewness coefficient as three times the difference between mean and median, divided by the standard deviation. It gauges the direction and degree of asymmetry in a distribution.
notes: A positive value indicates a right-skewed distribution and negative a left-skewed one; zero suggests symmetry. Requires s greater than zero and is sensitive to the median estimate.

name: z to Percentile (Logistic Approx)
description: Approximates the cumulative normal probability for a z-score using a logistic function with the scaling constant 1.702. It returns the fraction of a standard normal distribution below the given z.
notes: This is an approximation, not the exact normal CDF; error is small but grows in the tails. The result lies strictly between 0 and 1; z=0 gives exactly 0.5.

name: Sample Variance from Sum of Squares
description: Computes the sample variance using the computational form: the sum of squared values minus n times the squared mean, divided by n-1. It measures the spread of the data around the mean.
notes: Uses the n-1 (Bessel) divisor for an unbiased sample estimate, so n must be at least 2. Rounding error in sumsq or the mean can make small variances inaccurate.

name: Sturges' Rule (Histogram Bin Count)
description: Estimates the number of histogram bins to use for a dataset of size n with Sturges' rule, k = 1 + log2(n). It gives a simple, commonly used starting point for choosing bin counts.
notes: Works best for roughly normal, moderately sized datasets; for skewed or very large data other rules (e.g. Freedman-Diaconis) may fit better. The result is rounded to a whole number of bins.

name: Moving Average of the Last k Values
expression: sum(i, len(v) - k + 1, len(v), at(v, i)) / k
description: Averages the most recent k observations, the simplest smoothing and forecasting method.
notes: Lags behind trends by about (k − 1)/2 periods.

name: Sample Autocorrelation at Lag k
expression: sum(i, 1, len(v) - k, (at(v, i) - mean(v)) * (at(v, i + k) - mean(v))) / sum((v - mean(v))^2)
description: Measures how strongly a series correlates with itself k steps earlier; the building block of ARIMA identification.
notes: Values outside ±2/√n suggest real autocorrelation.

name: Relative Uncertainty of a Product or Quotient
description: Combines independent relative uncertainties for a result that is a product or quotient of measurements (GUM).
notes: Multiply by the result for its absolute uncertainty.

name: Uncertainty of a Power Law
description: Gives the relative uncertainty of xⁿ: the relative uncertainty of x multiplied by |n|.
notes: Cubing a length triples its relative error — why volume measurements are touchy.

name: Inverse-Variance Weighted Mean
description: Combines measurements of the same quantity, giving more weight to the more precise ones.
notes: Its uncertainty is 1/√Σ(1/σ²).

name: Uncertainty of the Weighted Mean
description: Gives the standard uncertainty of an inverse-variance weighted mean — smaller than any single measurement's.
notes: Adding a much worse measurement barely helps.

name: Reduced Chi-Square of a Fit
description: Judges a fit against the measurement uncertainties: about 1 is good, much larger means a poor model or underestimated errors.
notes: Much less than 1 suggests the errors were overestimated.

name: Expanded Uncertainty
description: Combines independent uncertainty components by root-sum-square and multiplies by a coverage factor (k = 2 ≈ 95 %) as in the GUM.
notes: Report as value ± U (k = 2).

name: Median of a Data List
description: Gives the middle value of a data set — robust to outliers, unlike the mean.
notes: For an even count it averages the two middle values.

name: Mode of a Data List
description: Gives the most frequent value in a data set (the smallest one if several tie).
notes: Most useful for discrete or categorical data.

name: Sample Standard Deviation of a Data List
description: Gives the sample standard deviation (dividing by n − 1) of a data set.
notes: Use the population version when the data are the whole population.

name: Population Standard Deviation of a Data List
description: Gives the standard deviation dividing by n, for data that are the whole population.
notes: Always slightly smaller than the sample version.

name: Standard Error of the Mean from Data
description: Gives how precisely the sample mean estimates the population mean.
notes: Quadrupling the sample halves the standard error.

name: Coefficient of Variation of a Data List
description: Gives the standard deviation as a percentage of the mean, to compare spread across different scales.
notes: Only meaningful for data on a ratio scale (true zero).

name: Trimmed Mean
expression: sum(i, floor(count(x) * tp) + 1, count(x) - floor(count(x) * tp), at(sort(x), i)) / (count(x) - 2 * floor(count(x) * tp))
description: Averages the data after dropping a fraction from each end, a compromise between mean and median.
notes: Used for judges' scores and the "trimmed mean" inflation measure.

name: Median Absolute Deviation (Scaled)
description: Gives a robust measure of spread; scaled by 1.4826 it estimates the standard deviation for normal data.
notes: A single wild value barely changes it.

name: Mean Absolute Deviation about the Mean
description: Gives the average distance of data points from their mean.
notes: Easier to explain than the standard deviation, but less convenient mathematically.

name: Quartile (Linear Interpolation)
description: Gives the first, second (median) or third quartile, interpolating between data points (the common spreadsheet method).
notes: Other definitions give slightly different values for small data sets.

name: Upper Outlier Fence (Tukey)
description: Gives the value above which points are flagged as outliers in a box plot (Tukey 1977).
notes: The lower fence is Q1 − 1.5·IQR; 3·IQR marks far outliers.

name: Bowley (Quartile) Skewness
description: Measures asymmetry from the quartiles, between −1 and 1; unaffected by extreme tails.
notes: Positive means a longer upper half.

name: Quartile Coefficient of Dispersion
description: Gives a robust, scale-free measure of spread from the quartiles.
notes: A robust alternative to the coefficient of variation.

name: Sample Skewness of a Data List
description: Gives the adjusted Fisher–Pearson skewness of a sample (as in spreadsheets' SKEW).
notes: Above about 1 in absolute value indicates strong skew.

name: Excess Kurtosis of a Data List
description: Gives the sample excess kurtosis (as in spreadsheets' KURT): 0 for normal data, positive for heavy tails.
notes: Sensitive to a few extreme values.

name: z-Score of a Value within a Data Set
description: Gives how many sample standard deviations a value lies from the data set's mean.
notes: Beyond ±3 is unusual for roughly normal data.

name: Midrange
description: Gives the average of the largest and smallest values.
notes: Very sensitive to outliers; used in quality control and weather records.

name: Index of Dispersion (Variance-to-Mean Ratio)
description: Compares the variance of counts with their mean: about 1 for Poisson (random) counts, above 1 for clustering.
notes: Used for spatial patterns and overdispersion checks.

name: Gini Coefficient of a Distribution
expression: sum(i, 1, count(x), (2 * i - count(x) - 1) * at(sort(x), i)) / (count(x) * sum(x))
description: Measures inequality among values: 0 when all are equal, approaching 1 when one holds everything.
notes: Countries' income Gini ranges from about 0.25 to 0.63.

name: Correlation Coefficient of Paired Data
description: Gives Pearson's r for two paired lists: +1 perfect positive, −1 perfect negative, 0 no linear relation.
notes: Correlation is not causation.

name: Sample Covariance of Paired Data
description: Gives the sample covariance (dividing by n − 1) of two paired lists.
notes: Its sign shows the direction of association; its size depends on the units.

name: Least-Squares Slope of Paired Data
description: Gives the slope of the best-fit straight line through paired data.
notes: Change in y per unit change in x.

name: Standard Error of the Regression
description: Gives the typical size of the residuals around a fitted straight line (n − 2 degrees of freedom).
notes: About 95 % of points lie within ±2 of these from the line.

name: Standard Error of a Regression Slope
description: Gives the uncertainty of a fitted slope; slope ÷ SE is the t statistic with n − 2 degrees of freedom.
notes: Spreading the x values out makes the slope more precise.

name: t-Statistic for a Correlation
description: Tests whether a sample correlation differs from zero; compare with t on n − 2 degrees of freedom.
notes: r = 0.45 with 30 pairs gives t ≈ 2.67 (p ≈ 0.013).

name: p-Value for a Correlation (Two-Sided)
description: Gives the two-sided p-value for testing a Pearson correlation against zero.
notes: Small samples need large r to be significant.

name: Confidence Interval for a Correlation (Lower)
description: Gives the lower confidence limit of a correlation using Fisher's z-transformation.
notes: The interval is asymmetric around r.

name: Mean of Grouped Data
description: Estimates the mean from a frequency table using class midpoints.
notes: Exact only if data sit at the midpoints.

name: Median of Grouped Data

variables.label: Lower boundary of the median class
Cumulative frequency before the median class

description: Estimates the median of grouped data by linear interpolation within the class that contains it.
notes: Find the median class first: where the cumulative frequency passes n/2.

name: Standard Deviation of Grouped Data
description: Estimates the sample standard deviation from a frequency table using class midpoints.
notes: Sheppard's correction can remove the grouping bias.

name: Geometric Mean of a Data List
description: Gives the n-th root of the product — the right average for growth rates and ratios.
notes: Always ≤ the arithmetic mean.

name: Harmonic Mean of a Data List

variables.label: Positive values (e.g. speeds over equal distances)

description: Gives the reciprocal of the mean of reciprocals — the right average for rates over equal amounts, such as speeds over equal distances.
notes: Always ≤ the geometric mean.

name: Root Mean Square of a Data List
description: Gives the square root of the mean of squares, the "effective" size of values that swing positive and negative.
notes: Used for AC signals, errors and noise.

name: Weighted Standard Deviation
description: Gives the (population-style) standard deviation of values with weights, e.g. frequencies or importance.
notes: For frequency weights and a sample estimate divide by Σw − 1 instead.

name: Overall F-Statistic of a Regression
description: Tests whether a multiple regression explains any variance at all, from its R².
notes: Compare with F(k, n − k − 1).

name: Variance Inflation Factor

variables.label: R² of predictor j on the other predictors

description: Measures how much collinearity inflates the variance of a regression coefficient.
notes: Above 5–10 signals problematic multicollinearity.

name: Standard Error of Estimate (Multiple Regression)
description: Gives the typical size of the residuals of a regression with k predictors.
notes: Same units as the response.

name: Prediction Interval Half-Width (Simple Regression)
expression: tinv(1 - al / 2, count(xp) - 2) * sqrt((1 - rsq(xp, y)) * var(y) * (count(y) - 1) / (count(y) - 2)) * sqrt(1 + 1 / count(xp) + (x0 - mean(xp))^2 / (var(xp) * (count(xp) - 1)))
description: Gives the ± range for a single new observation predicted at x₀ by a fitted line.
notes: Wider than the confidence band for the mean, and wider away from the data's centre.

name: Leverage of a Point (Simple Regression)
description: Gives the hat value of a point: how much it can pull the fitted line, larger at extreme x.
notes: Values above about 2(k + 1)/n deserve a look.

name: Cook's Distance
description: Measures how much all fitted values would change if one point were deleted (Cook 1977).
notes: Above about 4/n, or 1, marks an influential point.

name: Internally Studentised Residual
description: Scales a residual by its own standard error, allowing for leverage; beyond ±2–3 suggests an outlier.
notes: High-leverage points have smaller raw residuals.

name: Mallows' Cp
description: Compares subset regression models: a good model has Cp close to p (Mallows 1973).
notes: Much larger than p signals bias from missing predictors.

name: Partial Correlation (Controlling for One Variable)
description: Gives the correlation between x and y after removing the linear effect of z.
notes: Can change sign when z is a confounder.

name: Correlation Corrected for Attenuation
description: Estimates the correlation between true scores by removing the dilution caused by measurement error (Spearman 1904).
notes: Can exceed 1 if reliabilities are underestimated.

name: Regression to the Mean: Expected Retest Score
description: Gives the expected second measurement for someone who scored x the first time; extreme scores drift back towards the mean.
notes: Explains why "improvement" after selecting extreme cases can be illusory.

name: Logistic Regression Probability (Two Predictors)
description: Gives the predicted probability from a fitted logistic regression with two predictors.
notes: Each coefficient is a log-odds ratio.

name: Poisson Regression Expected Count
description: Gives the expected count from a Poisson (log-link) regression with an exposure offset.
notes: e^β₁ is the rate ratio per unit of x.

name: Holt's Linear Trend: Level Update
description: Updates the level in Holt's double exponential smoothing, which tracks a trend (Holt 1957).
notes: The trend then updates as β(ℓₜ − ℓₜ₋₁) + (1 − β)bₜ₋₁.

name: Holt's Linear Trend: h-Step Forecast
description: Gives Holt's forecast h steps ahead: current level plus h times the trend.
notes: Damped-trend variants avoid over-extrapolation.

name: Forecast Tracking Signal
description: Divides cumulative forecast error by mean absolute deviation; beyond about ±4 the forecast is biased.
notes: Used to monitor demand forecasts.

name: Geometric Standard Deviation
description: Gives the multiplicative spread of log-normal data: about 68 % lie between GM ÷ GSD and GM × GSD.
notes: Common for particle sizes and environmental concentrations.

name: Standard Deviation Estimated from the IQR
description: Estimates the standard deviation from an interquartile range, assuming normal data.
notes: Used in meta-analyses when only medians and IQRs are reported.
